newsitem.title: USA: Wherehouse reorganization plan is confirmed.
newsitem.headline: Wherehouse reorganization plan is confirmed.

text.p: Troubled music retailer Wherehouse Entertainment cleared a major hurdle Friday as its plan of reorganization was confirmed in U.S. Bankruptcy Court.

"The plan was confirmed. There had been objections filed by bondholders, but a settlement was reached with all the various creditor groups," said Elliott Cobb, treasurer of the 265-store chain that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in August 1995.
"We should emerge out of bankrupty in January and expect the company will be profitable in the fiscal year ending January 1998," he said.

The plan, which was put forth by Wherehouse and confirmed in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Delaware, assigned a value of $115 million to the chain, which has closed 81 stores since it filed for bankruptcy.

A Merrill Lynch investment fund bought the chain in 1992 in a $275 million leveraged buyout financed by paying $70 million in cash, issuing $110 million in bonds and obtaining a term loan from a banking consortium for the remainder.
The deal went sour, however, when a price war in the music retailing industry severely reduced the company's cash flow, which was one of the factors that contributed to its Chapter 11 filing.
Under the plan that was confirmed Friday, Cerberus Partners Ltd., an investment fund that bought up most of Wherehouse's senior bank debt in 1996 becomes a majority stockholder.

A group of vendors, primarily major record distributors, owed more than $46 million will receive about 27 cents on the dollar in new common stock in the company, which can be exchanged for cash if they agree to normal trade terms going forward, Cobb said.
Cobb said since September 1995, the company has had a debtor-in-posssession financing facility in place, allowing it to borrow up to $30 million.
The Torrance, Calif.-based retailer filed an amended plan in September, providing further details on how it would thrive in the difficult music sales environment.
"I think it's generally felt there is an overcapacity in the music retailing business and that a shakeout in the business could continue in the short-term," Cobb said.
Other music retailers have suffered similar woes, including 365-store Camelot Music Inc., which filed for bankruptcy in August.

The 793-store chain, Musicland Stores Corp., which is considered by record companies to be the top retailer, has had to close several stores. Industry sources said it also has received favorable credit terms from vendors to help it through the tough time.
Cobb said some of its venders had extended credit to the company, including the distributing arms of Time Warner Inc.'s Warner Music business, PolyGram NV and EMI Plc.
